claim: The Reissner fiber (RF) is an acellular thread positioned in the midline of the central canal.
source: The Reissner fiber (RF) is an acellular thread positioned in the midline of the central canal that aggregates thanks to the beating of numerous cilia from ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs) generating flow in the central canal of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of RF structure and location.

claim: RF aggregates thanks to the beating of numerous cilia from ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs) generating flow in the central canal of the spinal cord.
source: The Reissner fiber (RF) is an acellular thread positioned in the midline of the central canal that aggregates thanks to the beating of numerous cilia from ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs) generating flow in the central canal of the spinal cord.
evidence: This mechanism of RF aggregation is stated in the abstract.

claim: RF together with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) form an axial sensory system detecting curvature.
source: RF together with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) form an axial sensory system detecting curvature.
evidence: This functional relationship is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: RF is under tension in vivo.
source: Using in vivo imaging in larval zebrafish, we show that RF is under tension and resonates dorsoventrally.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: RF resonates dorsoventrally.
source: Using in vivo imaging in larval zebrafish, we show that RF is under tension and resonates dorsoventrally.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: Focal RF ablations trigger retraction and relaxation of the fiber's cut ends.
source: Focal RF ablations trigger retraction and relaxation of the fiber's cut ends, with larger retraction speeds for rostral ablations.
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the abstract.

claim: Larger retraction speeds occur for rostral ablations compared to other positions.
source: Focal RF ablations trigger retraction and relaxation of the fiber's cut ends, with larger retraction speeds for rostral ablations.
evidence: This is a specific finding from ablation experiments stated in the abstract.

claim: A mechanical model estimates RF stress diffusion coefficient D at 5 mm2/s.
source: We built a mechanical model that estimates RF stress diffusion coefficient D at 5 mm2/s and reveals that tension builds up rostrally along the fiber.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the mechanical model presented in the abstract.

claim: Tension builds up rostrally along the fiber.
source: We built a mechanical model that estimates RF stress diffusion coefficient D at 5 mm2/s and reveals that tension builds up rostrally along the fiber.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mechanical model stated in the abstract.

claim: After RF ablation, spontaneous CSF-cN activity decreased.
source: After RF ablation, spontaneous CSF-cN activity decreased and ciliary motility changed, suggesting physical interactions between RF and cilia projecting into the central canal.
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the abstract.

claim: After RF ablation, ciliary motility changed.
source: After RF ablation, spontaneous CSF-cN activity decreased and ciliary motility changed, suggesting physical interactions between RF and cilia projecting into the central canal.
evidence: This is an experimental observation stated in the abstract.

claim: Physical interactions occur between RF and cilia projecting into the central canal.
source: After RF ablation, spontaneous CSF-cN activity decreased and ciliary motility changed, suggesting physical interactions between RF and cilia projecting into the central canal.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of changes after RF ablation.

claim: Motile cilia were caudally-tilted.
source: We observed that motile cilia were caudally-tilted and frequently interacted with RF.
evidence: This is a direct observation stated in the abstract.

claim: Motile cilia frequently interacted with RF.
source: We observed that motile cilia were caudally-tilted and frequently interacted with RF.
evidence: This is a direct observation stated in the abstract.

claim: The numerous ependymal motile monocilia contribute to RF's heterogenous tension via weak interactions.
source: We propose that the numerous ependymal motile monocilia contribute to RF's heterogenous tension via weak interactions.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism stated in the abstract based on observations.

claim: Under tension, the Reissner fiber dynamically interacts with motile cilia generating CSF flow and spinal sensory neurons.
source: Our work demonstrates that under tension, the Reissner fiber dynamically interacts with motile cilia generating CSF flow and spinal sensory neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is secreted by the choroid plexuses.
source: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is secreted by the choroid plexuses and fills the intracerebral ventricles, spinal and brain subarachnoid spaces, and the central canal of the spinal cord (Lun et al., 2015; Battal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF fills the intracerebral ventricles, spinal and brain subarachnoid spaces, and the central canal of the spinal cord.
source: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is secreted by the choroid plexuses and fills the intracerebral ventricles, spinal and brain subarachnoid spaces, and the central canal of the spinal cord (Lun et al., 2015; Battal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The physico-chemical properties of the CSF impact the development of the nervous system by influencing neurogenesis.
source: In the last decade, the physico-chemical properties of the CSF have been shown to impact the development of the nervous system by influencing neurogenesis (Lehtinen et al., 2011), neuronal migration (Paul et al., 2017) as well as morphogenesis (Bearce and Grimes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The physico-chemical properties of the CSF impact the development of the nervous system by influencing neuronal migration.
source: In the last decade, the physico-chemical properties of the CSF have been shown to impact the development of the nervous system by influencing neurogenesis (Lehtinen et al., 2011), neuronal migration (Paul et al., 2017) as well as morphogenesis (Bearce and Grimes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The physico-chemical properties of the CSF impact the development of the nervous system by influencing morphogenesis.
source: In the last decade, the physico-chemical properties of the CSF have been shown to impact the development of the nervous system by influencing neurogenesis (Lehtinen et al., 2011), neuronal migration (Paul et al., 2017) as well as morphogenesis (Bearce and Grimes, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish, the circulation of CSF modulates the geometry of the body axis during embryogenesis.
source: In zebrafish, the circulation of CSF modulates the geometry of the body axis during embryogenesis (Zhang et al., 2018) and spine curvature in juvenile/adult zebrafish (Grimes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish, the circulation of CSF modulates spine curvature in juvenile/adult zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, the circulation of CSF modulates the geometry of the body axis during embryogenesis (Zhang et al., 2018) and spine curvature in juvenile/adult zebrafish (Grimes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Straight body axis formation and spine organogenesis rely on the expression of urotensin neuropeptides in the spinal cord by ciliated sensory neurons surrounding the central canal.
source: Genetic investigations in zebrafish revealed that straight body axis formation and spine organogenesis rely on the expression of urotensin neuropeptides in the spinal cord by ciliated sensory neurons surrounding the central canal, referred to as CSF-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) (Quan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Bearce et al., 2022; Gaillard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spinal CSF-cNs were identified by Kolmer and Agduhr in over a hundred vertebrate species.
source: Spinal CSF-cNs were identified by Kolmer and Agduhr in over a hundred vertebrate species (Kolmer, 1921; Agduhr, 1922; Vigh and Vigh-Teichmann, 1998) as GABAergic sensory neurons that project an apical extension into the lumen of the central canal and extend an ascending axon into the spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cNs are GABAergic sensory neurons that project an apical extension into the lumen of the central canal and extend an ascending axon into the spinal cord.
source: Spinal CSF-cNs were identified by Kolmer and Agduhr in over a hundred vertebrate species (Kolmer, 1921; Agduhr, 1922; Vigh and Vigh-Teichmann, 1998) as GABAergic sensory neurons that project an apical extension into the lumen of the central canal and extend an ascending axon into the spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apical extension of CSF-cNs comprises one motile cilium and a brush of microvilli that bathe in the CSF.
source: The apical extension comprises one motile cilium and a brush of microvilli that bathe in the CSF (Vigh and Vigh-Teichmann, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: During development, CSF-cNs differentiate into dorsolateral and ventral populations that are distinguished by distinct developmental origins.
source: During development, CSF-cNs differentiate into dorsolateral and ventral populations that are distinguished by distinct developmental origins (Park et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2012; Petracca et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cN populations differ by the morphology of their ciliated apical extension and axonal projections.
source: These two populations differ by the morphology of their ciliated apical extension and axonal projections, their expression of peptides (Quan et al., 2015; Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Prendergast et al., 2023) as well as the neuronal targets contacted by the CSF-cN axons (Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cN populations differ by their expression of peptides.
source: These two populations differ by the morphology of their ciliated apical extension and axonal projections, their expression of peptides (Quan et al., 2015; Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Prendergast et al., 2023) as well as the neuronal targets contacted by the CSF-cN axons (Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cN populations differ by the neuronal targets contacted by the CSF-cN axons.
source: These two populations differ by the morphology of their ciliated apical extension and axonal projections, their expression of peptides (Quan et al., 2015; Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Prendergast et al., 2023) as well as the neuronal targets contacted by the CSF-cN axons (Djenoune et al., 2017; Desban et al., 2019; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cNs express urotensin-related peptides under the control of the Reissner Fiber (RF).
source: CSF-cNs express urotensin-related peptides under the control of the Reissner Fiber (RF) (Quan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020), an acellular thread bathing in CSF within the lumen of the central canal and in close vicinity to the apical extension of CSF-cNs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RF is an acellular thread bathing in CSF within the lumen of the central canal and in close vicinity to the apical extension of CSF-cNs.
source: CSF-cNs express urotensin-related peptides under the control of the Reissner Fiber (RF) (Quan et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020), an acellular thread bathing in CSF within the lumen of the central canal and in close vicinity to the apical extension of CSF-cNs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RF forms during development from the aggregation of the monomer SCO-spondin, a very large glycoprotein.
source: Thanks to the beating of the numerous motile monocilia from ependymal radial glia, RF forms during development from the aggregation of the monomer SCO-spondin, a very large glycoprotein (Sterba et al., 1982; Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SCO-spondin is initially secreted into the CSF by cells in the floor plate, the flexural organ and the subcommissural organ (SCO).
source: SCO-spondin is initially secreted into the CSF by cells in the floor plate, the flexural organ and the subcommissural organ (SCO), and is later solely produced by the SCO (Meiniel and Meiniel, 2007; Gobron et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SCO-spondin is later solely produced by the SCO.
source: SCO-spondin is initially secreted into the CSF by cells in the floor plate, the flexural organ and the subcommissural organ (SCO), and is later solely produced by the SCO (Meiniel and Meiniel, 2007; Gobron et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In larval zebrafish, RF diameter is approximately 200 nm.
source: In larval zebrafish, RF diameter is approximately 200 nm (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and RF displays slow, continual rostrocaudal movement (Troutwine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: RF displays slow, continual rostrocaudal movement.
source: In larval zebrafish, RF diameter is approximately 200 nm (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and RF displays slow, continual rostrocaudal movement (Troutwine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In mutant embryos for scospondin in which RF does not form, the body axis is curled down.
source: In mutant embryos for scospondin in which RF does not form, the body axis is curled down (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In scospondin mutants in which RF forms in the embryo but is not maintained in juvenile stages, the body axis becomes straight during embryogenesis, but later at the juvenile stage the spine undergoes 3D torsion, a hallmark of idiopathic scoliosis.
source: Furthermore, in scospondin mutants in which RF forms in the embryo but is not maintained in juvenile stages (Troutwine et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2020), the body axis becomes straight during embryogenesis, but later on at the juvenile stage the spine undergoes 3D torsion, a hallmark of idiopathic scoliosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Peptides from the family of urotensin (Urp1, Urp2) and their receptor Uts2r3 play a major role in straightening the body axis throughout life.
source: Peptides from the family of urotensin (Urp1, Urp2) and their receptor Uts2r3 play a major role in straightening the body axis throughout life (Bearce et al., 2022; Gaillard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Urotensin signaling is relevant in human patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
source: Remarkably, urotensin signaling is relevant in human patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Dai et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cNs sense zebrafish body curvature in vivo.
source: We previously showed that CSF-cNs sense zebrafish body curvature in vivo (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CSF-cNs can respond in vitro to pressure-application in an open book preparation of the lamprey spinal cord.
source: Accordingly, CSF-cNs can respond in vitro to pressure-application in an open book preparation of the lamprey spinal cord (Jalalvand et al., 2016) as well as to mechanical stimulation applied to CSF-cN cell membranes in primary cultures (Sternberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cNs can respond to mechanical stimulation applied to CSF-cN cell membranes in primary cultures.
source: Accordingly, CSF-cNs can respond in vitro to pressure-application in an open book preparation of the lamprey spinal cord (Jalalvand et al., 2016) as well as to mechanical stimulation applied to CSF-cN cell membranes in primary cultures (Sternberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs sense spinal curvature in vivo only on the concave side.
source: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs sense spinal curvature in vivo only on the concave side (Böhm et al., 2016), a process that requires intact Pkd2l1 channels.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CSF-cN sensing of spinal curvature requires intact Pkd2l1 channels.
source: In zebrafish, CSF-cNs sense spinal curvature in vivo only on the concave side (Böhm et al., 2016), a process that requires intact Pkd2l1 channels.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CSF-cN sensing of spinal curvature relies on a modulation of the opening probability of the mechanosensory channel Pkd2l1 for CSF-cNs on the concave side, ipsilateral to where skeletal muscles contract.
source: This process relies on a modulation of the opening probability of the mechanosensory channel Pkd2l1 (Sternberg et al., 2018) for CSF-cNs on the concave side, ipsilateral to where skeletal muscles contract (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish lacking RF, both the CSF flow and Pkd2l1 channel activity are unaffected.
source: In zebrafish lacking RF, both the CSF flow (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and Pkd2l1 channel activity (Sternberg et al., 2018) are unaffected, yet CSF-cN response to spinal curvature was reduced (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish lacking RF, CSF-cN response to spinal curvature was reduced.
source: In zebrafish lacking RF, both the CSF flow (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and Pkd2l1 channel activity (Sternberg et al., 2018) are unaffected, yet CSF-cN response to spinal curvature was reduced (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: An intact RF amplifies the mechanosensitivity of CSF-cNs.
source: These observations suggest that an intact RF amplifies the mechanosensitivity of CSF-cNs, either by RF contacting the ciliated CSF-cN apical extension or by enhancing the gradient of CSF flow that CSF-cNs are subject to during spinal bending.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the introduction based on cited observations.

claim: Previous investigations on the structure of RF and its interaction with CSF-cNs were performed in fixed tissues.
source: Previous investigations on the structure of RF and its interaction with CSF-cNs were performed in fixed tissues (using 4% paraformaldehyde; see Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020), which leads to deformation of the central canal that can alter the relative distance of the RF to CSF-cNs (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020; Thouvenin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Fixation leads to deformation of the central canal that can alter the relative distance of the RF to CSF-cNs.
source: Previous investigations on the structure of RF and its interaction with CSF-cNs were performed in fixed tissues (using 4% paraformaldehyde; see Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018; Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020), which leads to deformation of the central canal that can alter the relative distance of the RF to CSF-cNs (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020; Thouvenin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RF was straight and taut in the sagittal plane in 3 dpf Tg(sspo:sspo-GFP) larvae after paralysis.
source: In 3 days post fertilization (dpf) Tg(sspo:sspo-GFP) larvae after paralysis (see Materials and methods), we observed that RF was straight and taut in the sagittal plane and rapidly changed position along the dorsoventral axis over time in the central canal (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: RF rapidly changed position along the dorsoventral axis over time in the central canal.
source: In 3 days post fertilization (dpf) Tg(sspo:sspo-GFP) larvae after paralysis (see Materials and methods), we observed that RF was straight and taut in the sagittal plane and rapidly changed position along the dorsoventral axis over time in the central canal (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: RF of larvae after fixation was slack and stationary.
source: In contrast, RF of larvae after fixation was slack and stationary (Figure 1C; see also Video 1 in paralyzed live larvae, Video 2 after fixation, Video 3 in unparalyzed live larvae).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1C and Videos 1-3.

claim: The dorsoventral displacement of the fiber from its mean position in the central canal was on average 74 nm ± 68 nm in paralyzed living larvae.
source: We estimated that the dorsoventral displacement of the fiber from its mean position in the central canal (on average median ± standard deviation for all values provided hereafter: 74 nm ± 68 nm) was significantly larger in paralyzed living larvae than in euthanized larvae after fixation (on average: 32 nm ± 39 nm; unpaired two-tailed t-test: p < 10-4; Figure 1F1)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments shown in Figure 1F1.

claim: The dorsoventral displacement of the fiber from its mean position in the central canal was on average 32 nm ± 39 nm in euthanized larvae after fixation.
source: We estimated that the dorsoventral displacement of the fiber from its mean position in the central canal (on average median ± standard deviation for all values provided hereafter: 74 nm ± 68 nm) was significantly larger in paralyzed living larvae than in euthanized larvae after fixation (on average: 32 nm ± 39 nm; unpaired two-tailed t-test: p < 10-4; Figure 1F1)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments shown in Figure 1F1.

claim: The dorsoventral displacement of RF was significantly larger in paralyzed living larvae than in euthanized larvae after fixation (p < 10-4).
source: We estimated that the dorsoventral displacement of the fiber from its mean position in the central canal (on average median ± standard deviation for all values provided hereafter: 74 nm ± 68 nm) was significantly larger in paralyzed living larvae than in euthanized larvae after fixation (on average: 32 nm ± 39 nm; unpaired two-tailed t-test: p < 10-4; Figure 1F1)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the experiments shown in Figure 1F1.

claim: The amplitude of RF dorsoventral displacement was largest in the middle portion (125 nm ± 108 nm).
source: The amplitude of RF dorsoventral displacement was largest in the middle portion (125 nm ± 108 nm), followed by the fiber displacement on the rostral side (100 nm ± 103 nm; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons: p < 10-4; Figure 1F1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments shown in Figure 1F1.

claim: The amplitude of RF dorsoventral displacement on the rostral side was 100 nm ± 103 nm.
source: The amplitude of RF dorsoventral displacement was largest in the middle portion (125 nm ± 108 nm), followed by the fiber displacement on the rostral side (100 nm ± 103 nm; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons: p < 10-4; Figure 1F1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments shown in Figure 1F1.

claim: The median of the amplitudes of RF displacement in the caudal end was 70 nm ± 68 nm.
source: The median of the amplitudes of RF displacement in the caudal end (70 nm ± 68 nm; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons: p < 10-4; Figure 1F2) was the closest to the fiber displacement of fixed larvae, possibly partly reflecting that the fiber is anchored on both the rostral and caudal ends of the fish.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments shown in Figure 1F2.

claim: The fiber is anchored on both the rostral and caudal ends of the fish.
source: The median of the amplitudes of RF displacement in the caudal end (70 nm ± 68 nm; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons: p < 10-4; Figure 1F2) was the closest to the fiber displacement of fixed larvae, possibly partly reflecting that the fiber is anchored on both the rostral and caudal ends of the fish.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caudal displacement is closest to fixed larvae.

claim: The first two principal components after dimensionality reduction represented dorsoventral translation and local rotation of the fiber, respectively.
source: Performing a spatial principal component analysis over all pixels in the video revealed that the first two components after dimensionality reduction represented dorsoventral translation and local rotation of the fiber, respectively (Figure 1G; see also Video 4).
evidence: This is a result from the principal component analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Fewer CSF-cN cells were active after RF photoablation (on average 11% compared to 28%; paired two-tailed t-test: p < 0.05).
source: Overall, fewer cells were active after RF photoablation (on average 11% compared to 28%; paired two-tailed t-test: p < 0.05; Figure 2C), and calcium activity decreased by 45% on average across larvae (Figure 2D), with a subset of ventral CSF-cNs showing decreased activity after RF photoablation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Calcium activity decreased by 45% on average across larvae after RF photoablation.
source: Overall, fewer cells were active after RF photoablation (on average 11% compared to 28%; paired two-tailed t-test: p < 0.05; Figure 2C), and calcium activity decreased by 45% on average across larvae (Figure 2D), with a subset of ventral CSF-cNs showing decreased activity after RF photoablation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of calcium events occurring within active CSF-cN cells decreased after RF ablation (on average 0.94 events/min before and 0.87 events/min after; paired two-tailed t-test: p < 0.005).
source: The number of calcium events occurring within those cells decreased after RF ablation (Figure 2E, on average 0.94 events/min before and 0.87 events/min after in active cells; paired two-tailed t-test: p < 0.005).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The presence of an intact RF in the central canal enhances the spontaneous calcium activity of ventral CSF-cNs.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that the presence of an intact RF in the central canal enhances the spontaneous calcium activity of ventral CSF-cNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium imaging experiments after RF ablation.

claim: The majority of fiber retractions (88% of 148 total retractions) demonstrated complete fiber retraction out of the 97 μm-wide field of view in less than 500 ms.
source: The majority of fiber retractions (88% of 148 total retractions, Figure 3A1 and A2) demonstrated complete fiber retraction out of the 97 μm-wide field of view in less than 500 ms (initial retraction speed of on average ~328 μm/s), with 96% of fibers remaining straight as the cut ends of the fiber retracted to the rostral and caudal ends of the larvae.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Initial retraction speed of RF after ablation was on average ~328 μm/s for fast retractions.
source: The majority of fiber retractions (88% of 148 total retractions, Figure 3A1 and A2) demonstrated complete fiber retraction out of the 97 μm-wide field of view in less than 500 ms (initial retraction speed of on average ~328 μm/s), with 96% of fibers remaining straight as the cut ends of the fiber retracted to the rostral and caudal ends of the larvae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 96% of fibers remained straight as the cut ends of the fiber retracted to the rostral and caudal ends of the larvae.
source: The majority of fiber retractions (88% of 148 total retractions, Figure 3A1 and A2) demonstrated complete fiber retraction out of the 97 μm-wide field of view in less than 500 ms (initial retraction speed of on average ~328 μm/s), with 96% of fibers remaining straight as the cut ends of the fiber retracted to the rostral and caudal ends of the larvae.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In 12% of 148 total retractions, the two cut ends of the fiber relaxed very slowly (initial retraction speed of on average ~50 μm/s).
source: However, in a few cases (12% of 148 total retractions, Figure 3B) we observed the two cut ends of the fiber relax very slowly (initial retraction speed of on average ~50 μm/s), often with the cut ends remaining still in the field of view for over 20 s (Figure 3C1–3C3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In a third of slow-retracting cases, slow-retracting ablated fibers displayed at the tip snake-like deformations during their relaxation.
source: In a third of these relaxed cases, we could observe that slow-retracting ablated fibers displayed at the tip snake-like deformations during their relaxation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When ablations occurred in the rostral side, only fast retraction kinetics were observed (N=105 fiber retractions).
source: When ablations occurred in the rostral side, we only observed fast retraction kinetics (N=105 fiber retractions, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ablations in the middle and caudal somites showed slower relaxation speeds.
source: In contrast, ablations in the middle and caudal somites showed slower relaxation speeds (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The retraction speed for the rostral and caudal cut ends of a given fiber were highly correlated in individual larvae (y = 0.9x + 2; R2 = 0.7; simple linear correlation: p < 10-4).
source: The retraction speed for the rostral and caudal cut ends of a given fiber were highly correlated in individual larvae despite the diversity of retraction patterns observed overall across fish (y = 0.9x + 2; R2 = 0.7; simple linear correlation: p < 10-4; Figure 3D), indicating that the retraction kinematics after ablation reveals the inherent physical properties of the fiber and the tension applied on it that differs as a function of the rostrocaudal position.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The retraction kinematics after ablation reveals the inherent physical properties of the fiber and the tension applied on it that differs as a function of the rostrocaudal position.
source: The retraction speed for the rostral and caudal cut ends of a given fiber were highly correlated in individual larvae despite the diversity of retraction patterns observed overall across fish (y = 0.9x + 2; R2 = 0.7; simple linear correlation: p < 10-4; Figure 3D), indicating that the retraction kinematics after ablation reveals the inherent physical properties of the fiber and the tension applied on it that differs as a function of the rostrocaudal position.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation observed in the RF ablation experiments.

claim: Maximum retraction speeds were greater in the rostral somites of the larvae (on average ± standard deviation: 448 μm/s ± 168 μm/s) than those in the middle or caudal somites (253 μm/s ± 166 μm/s and 211 μm/s ± 165 μm/s, respectively; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons; p < 10-4).
source: Accordingly, maximum retraction speeds were greater in the rostral somites of the larvae (on average ± standard deviation for all values provided hereafter: 448 μm/s ± 168 μm/s) than those in the middle or caudal somites (253 μm/s ± 166 μm/s and 211 μm/s ± 165 μm/s, respectively; Tukey's HSD Test for multiple comparisons; p < 10-4; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The Young's modulus of biopolymers of the cytoskeleton ranges from 1 to 4 GPa.
source: Estimation of the Young's modulus of biopolymers of the cytoskeleton gives E ranging from 1 to 4 GPa (Brochard-Wyart et al., 2019), a thousand times stiffer than the RF.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation for comparison with RF.

claim: The RF in larval zebrafish can be described as a soft elastic polymer that is maintained under tension in the CSF.
source: Overall, the RF in larval zebrafish can be described as a soft elastic polymer that is maintained under tension in the CSF and exhibits a mechanical diffusion coefficient of about 5 mm2/s, a characteristic time in the order of 2 ns and an elastic modulus of 106 Pascal – a value that would correspond to rubber rather than a rigid proteinaceous fiber.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the mechanical model and experimental data.

claim: RF exhibits a mechanical diffusion coefficient of about 5 mm2/s.
source: Overall, the RF in larval zebrafish can be described as a soft elastic polymer that is maintained under tension in the CSF and exhibits a mechanical diffusion coefficient of about 5 mm2/s, a characteristic time in the order of 2 ns and an elastic modulus of 106 Pascal – a value that would correspond to rubber rather than a rigid proteinaceous fiber.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the mechanical model and experimental data.

claim: RF exhibits a characteristic time in the order of 2 ns.

claim: Ciliated cells in contact with the CSF include CSF-cNs, which project a short motile kinocilium.
source: Ciliated cells in contact with the CSF include CSF-cNs, which project a short motile kinocilium (Böhm et al., 2016) and are known to be about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), as well as ependymal radial glial cells, which project a longer monocilium (Borovina et al., 2010; Becker and Becker, 2015) and are estimated via electron mictroscopy (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and the transgenic Tg(ß-actin:Arl13b-GFP) line Sternberg et al., 2018 to have a density of about 60 cilia per 10 μm along the 3.5 mm-long central canal, encompassing at least ~20,000 cilia at this stage.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: CSF-cNs are about a hundred at the 3 dpf stage.
source: Ciliated cells in contact with the CSF include CSF-cNs, which project a short motile kinocilium (Böhm et al., 2016) and are known to be about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), as well as ependymal radial glial cells, which project a longer monocilium (Borovina et al., 2010; Becker and Becker, 2015) and are estimated via electron mictroscopy (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and the transgenic Tg(ß-actin:Arl13b-GFP) line Sternberg et al., 2018 to have a density of about 60 cilia per 10 μm along the 3.5 mm-long central canal, encompassing at least ~20,000 cilia at this stage.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Ependymal radial glial cells project a longer monocilium.
source: Ciliated cells in contact with the CSF include CSF-cNs, which project a short motile kinocilium (Böhm et al., 2016) and are known to be about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), as well as ependymal radial glial cells, which project a longer monocilium (Borovina et al., 2010; Becker and Becker, 2015) and are estimated via electron mictroscopy (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and the transgenic Tg(ß-actin:Arl13b-GFP) line Sternberg et al., 2018 to have a density of about 60 cilia per 10 μm along the 3.5 mm-long central canal, encompassing at least ~20,000 cilia at this stage.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ependymal radial glial cells have a density of about 60 cilia per 10 μm along the 3.5 mm-long central canal, encompassing at least ~20,000 cilia at the 3 dpf stage.
source: Ciliated cells in contact with the CSF include CSF-cNs, which project a short motile kinocilium (Böhm et al., 2016) and are known to be about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), as well as ependymal radial glial cells, which project a longer monocilium (Borovina et al., 2010; Becker and Becker, 2015) and are estimated via electron mictroscopy (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020) and the transgenic Tg(ß-actin:Arl13b-GFP) line Sternberg et al., 2018 to have a density of about 60 cilia per 10 μm along the 3.5 mm-long central canal, encompassing at least ~20,000 cilia at this stage.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Immunohistochemistry staining against glutamylated tubulin and GFP showed that motile cilia are densely packed along the dorsal and ventral walls of the central canal and are oriented with a caudal tilt.
source: Immunohistochemistry staining against glutamylated tubulin and GFP showed that motile cilia are densely packed along the dorsal and ventral walls of the central canal and are oriented with a caudal tilt (Figure 4B1).
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 4B1.

claim: In contrast to the embryo, in which only ventral cilia are motile and tilted towards the caudal end, motile cilia in 3 dpf larvae are located both on the ventral and dorsal walls of the central canal.
source: In contrast to the embryo, in which only ventral cilia are motile and tilted towards the caudal end (Thouvenin et al., 2020), we observed that motile cilia in 3 dpf larvae are located both on the ventral and dorsal walls of the central canal at larval stage (Figure 4B2; see also Video 10).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging experiments shown in Figure 4B2, with a citation for comparison.

claim: Numerous motile cilia brushed against RF in sweeping motions.
source: When we took a closer look at isolated motile cilia labeled in 3 dpf Tg(β-actin:Arl13b-GFP) larvae and beating in the sagittal plane of imaging (see Materials and methods), we observed that numerous motile cilia brushed against RF in sweeping motions (Figure 4B2, C1 and D1; see also star symbol in Video 10), while others appear to almost stick to RF with a glob of fluorescent material at their tip (Figure 4C2 and D2; see also Video 10).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging experiments shown in Figure 4 and Video 10.

claim: Some motile cilia appear to almost stick to RF with a glob of fluorescent material at their tip.
source: When we took a closer look at isolated motile cilia labeled in 3 dpf Tg(β-actin:Arl13b-GFP) larvae and beating in the sagittal plane of imaging (see Materials and methods), we observed that numerous motile cilia brushed against RF in sweeping motions (Figure 4B2, C1 and D1; see also star symbol in Video 10), while others appear to almost stick to RF with a glob of fluorescent material at their tip (Figure 4C2 and D2; see also Video 10).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging experiments shown in Figure 4 and Video 10.

claim: Dorsal inserted cilia have an overall tilt towards the caudal end (mean ± standard deviation: 64.8° ± 44.4°; N=49 cilia across 8 fish).
source: We quantified the orientation of cilia in an angle relative to the horizontal (Figure 4E and F), and observed an overall tilt towards the caudal end both for dorsal inserted cilia (mean ± standard deviation provided hereafter: 64.8° ± 44.4°; N=49 cilia across 8 fish) and ventral inserted cilia (43.9° ± 35.8°; N=27 cilia across 9 fish; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cilia orientation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ventral inserted cilia have an overall tilt towards the caudal end (mean ± standard deviation: 43.9° ± 35.8°; N=27 cilia across 9 fish).
source: We quantified the orientation of cilia in an angle relative to the horizontal (Figure 4E and F), and observed an overall tilt towards the caudal end both for dorsal inserted cilia (mean ± standard deviation provided hereafter: 64.8° ± 44.4°; N=49 cilia across 8 fish) and ventral inserted cilia (43.9° ± 35.8°; N=27 cilia across 9 fish; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cilia orientation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The main ciliary beating frequency was estimated to be on average 11.2 Hz ± 2.4 Hz overall.
source: We estimated the main ciliary beating frequency to be on average 11.2 Hz ± 2.4 Hz overall (Figure 4H; dorsal: 11.8 Hz ± 2.7 Hz; ventral: 11.6 Hz ± 2.8 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cilia beating frequency analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The main ciliary beating frequency for dorsal cilia was 11.8 Hz ± 2.7 Hz.
source: We estimated the main ciliary beating frequency to be on average 11.2 Hz ± 2.4 Hz overall (Figure 4H; dorsal: 11.8 Hz ± 2.7 Hz; ventral: 11.6 Hz ± 2.8 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cilia beating frequency analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The main ciliary beating frequency for ventral cilia was 11.6 Hz ± 2.8 Hz.
source: We estimated the main ciliary beating frequency to be on average 11.2 Hz ± 2.4 Hz overall (Figure 4H; dorsal: 11.8 Hz ± 2.7 Hz; ventral: 11.6 Hz ± 2.8 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cilia beating frequency analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The tilt of cilia was not significantly different after RF photoablation (mean ± standard deviation: 55.1° ± 39.3°) from that before RF photoablation (57.4° ± 42.5°; N=76 cilia from 9 fish; paired two-tailed t-test: p > 0.3).
source: The tilt of cilia was not significantly different after RF photoablation (mean ± standard deviation provided hereafter: 55.1° ± 39.3°) from that before RF photoablation (57.4° ± 42.5°), illustrating that cilia orientation was, on average, not significantly affected by RF photoablation (Figure 4J; N=76 cilia from 9 fish; paired two-tailed t-test: p > 0.3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The impact of acute RF photoablation on ciliary beating frequency showed different responses among individuals.
source: In contrast, the impact of acute RF photoablation on ciliary beating frequency showed different responses among individuals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
evidence: This is an observation from the RF ablation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motile cilia densely surround the fiber along the walls of the central canal and brush along the fiber with a caudal tilt.
source: The fact that motile cilia densely surround the fiber along the walls of the central canal and brush along the fiber with a caudal tilt suggests that cilia-fiber interactions may generate friction promoting the oscillatory deflections of RF observed in vivo (Figure 1) and the deformations of the 'flower' ends of the cut RF during RF relaxation after photoablation (Figure 3B, B1 and B2).
evidence: This is an observation that leads to a suggested mechanism.

claim: Cilia-fiber interactions may generate friction promoting the oscillatory deflections of RF observed in vivo.
source: The fact that motile cilia densely surround the fiber along the walls of the central canal and brush along the fiber with a caudal tilt suggests that cilia-fiber interactions may generate friction promoting the oscillatory deflections of RF observed in vivo (Figure 1) and the deformations of the 'flower' ends of the cut RF during RF relaxation after photoablation (Figure 3B, B1 and B2).
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism based on observations.

claim: A minority of cilia (N=7/15 dorsal and N=4/9 ventral) show significant differences in their beating orientation depending on the up or down position of RF.
source: While dorsal and ventral motile cilia position profiles differ with RF dorsoventral oscillation position, a minority of cilia (N=7/15 dorsal and N=4/9 ventral) show significant differences in their beating orientation depending on the up or down position of RF (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B1, B2; Fisher's exact test: p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 for dorsal and ventral example cilia, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both dorsal and ventral cilia were closer to the vertical orientation when the fiber was down compared to when it is up (mean ± standard deviation: 60° ± 10° when RF down versus 48° ± 16° when RF up for dorsal cilia, and 55° ± 23° when RF down versus 33° ± 16° when RF up for ventral cilia).
source: Of these cilia, both dorsal and ventral cilia were closer to the vertical orientation when the fiber was down compared to when it is up (mean ± standard deviation from hereafter: 60° ± 10° when RF down versus 48° ± 16° when RF up for dorsal cilia, and 55° ± 23° when RF down versus 33° ± 16° when RF up for ventral cilia; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The Reissner fiber is a dynamic structure under tension in vivo in the central canal with elastic properties and spontaneous oscillatory activity.
source: Our work reveals that the Reissner fiber (RF) is a dynamic structure under tension in vivo in the central canal with elastic properties and spontaneous oscillatory activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: The Reissner fiber in larval zebrafish can be described as a soft elastic polymer that is maintained under tension in the CSF and exhibits a mechanical diffusion coefficient of 5 mm2/s, a characteristic time in the order of 2 ns and an elastic modulus of 106 Pascal, which would fit more with the fiber acting as a low density gel rather than a rigid proteinaceous fiber.
source: Our mechanical model reveals that the Reissner fiber in larval zebrafish can be described as a soft elastic polymer that is maintained under tension in the CSF and exhibits a mechanical diffusion coefficient of 5 mm2/s, a characteristic time in the order of 2 ns and an elastic modulus of 106 Pascal, which would fit more with the fiber acting as a low density gel rather than a rigid proteinaceous fiber.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: At baseline, in paralyzed animals with a straight body axis, the Reissner fiber interacts with the numerous long, beating monocilia of ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs).
source: At baseline, in paralyzed animals with a straight body axis, we found evidence that the Reissner fiber interacts with the numerous long, beating monocilia of ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs), which we estimated to have a density of at least 20,000 cilia at this stage (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020; Sternberg et al., 2018) as well as with some ciliated sensory neurons (CSF-cNs), known to be only about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), whose activity decreases upon photoablation of the fiber.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: At baseline, in paralyzed animals with a straight body axis, the Reissner fiber interacts with some ciliated sensory neurons (CSF-cNs), whose activity decreases upon photoablation of the fiber.
source: At baseline, in paralyzed animals with a straight body axis, we found evidence that the Reissner fiber interacts with the numerous long, beating monocilia of ependymal radial glial cells (ERGs), which we estimated to have a density of at least 20,000 cilia at this stage (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020; Sternberg et al., 2018) as well as with some ciliated sensory neurons (CSF-cNs), known to be only about a hundred at this stage (Prendergast et al., 2023), whose activity decreases upon photoablation of the fiber.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: RF being rectilinear contrasts with observations in the tissue after fixation, in which it curls and bends across the rostrocaudal axis.
source: By investigating the dynamical properties of the Reissner fiber in the central canal, we observed that the fiber is under tension in vivo, confirming previous observations of RF being rectilinear (Troutwine et al., 2020), which contrasts with observations in the tissue after fixation, in which it curls and bends across the rostrocaudal axis (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: RF can be modeled as a taut polymer under a heterogeneous tension in vivo.
source: Our observations demonstrate that RF can be modeled as a taut polymer under a heterogeneous tension in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on experimental observations.

claim: RF displays spontaneous oscillatory activity over the dorsoventral axis in addition to the spontaneous slow translation along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: In addition to the spontaneous slow translation of RF previously observed along the rostrocaudal axis with material continually added and retracted from its surface (Troutwine et al., 2020), our observations further reveal spontaneous oscillatory activity of the fiber over the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Large spontaneous oscillatory activity of RF occurs in the middle portion of the fish, away from the attachment points in the rostral end (SCO) and caudal end (ampulla caudalis).
source: We observe large spontaneous oscillatory activity of RF in the middle portion of the fish, away from the attachment points in the rostral end (SCO) and caudal end (ampulla caudalis) (Meiniel and Meiniel, 2007; Gobron et al., 2000), akin to oscillatory behaviors of a plucked guitar string.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The dorsoventral oscillations of the fiber probably occur at higher frequency than the 20 Hz observed in the experimental conditions.
source: To capture enough photons from the GFP-tagged fiber in our recordings, we sampled displacements of the fiber along the dorsoventral axis at 40 Hz at most. However, we have indications that the dorsoventral oscillations of the fiber probably occur at higher frequency than the 20 Hz we could observe in these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the experimental setup.

claim: The coordinated beating of motile cilia in the central canal has been reported up to 45 Hz, generating CSF flow estimated at a velocity of 10 μm/s in the embryo.
source: Previously, the coordinated beating of motile cilia in the central canal has been reported up to 45 Hz, generating CSF flow estimated at a velocity of 10 μm/s in the embryo (Thouvenin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Beating of cilia may influence locally how the Reissner fiber oscillates across the dorsoventral axis.
source: Such beating of cilia may influence locally how the Reissner fiber oscillates across the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion.

claim: Interactions between motile cilia and the fiber may contribute to maintaining the fiber under tension, with graded tension on the rostral end.
source: Furthermore, interactions between motile cilia and the fiber may contribute to maintaining the fiber under tension, with graded tension on the rostral end.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion.

claim: The faster retraction speeds observed after fiber ablation on the rostral side reveals that the pulling force on the fiber may not be uniform along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: In contrast, the faster retraction speeds observed after fiber ablation on the rostral side reveals that the pulling force on the fiber may not be uniform along the rostrocaudal axis.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion based on experimental observations.

claim: A higher tension in the rostral portion may be due to external factors increasing tension on the rostral side, such as the CSF flow going in the rostrocaudal direction and/or the friction associated with the numerous interactions occurring between the fiber and the beating cilia along the central canal.
source: A higher tension in the rostral portion may be due to external factors increasing tension on the rostral side, such as the CSF flow going in the rostrocaudal direction (Tumani et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018) and/or the friction associated with the numerous interactions occurring between the fiber and the beating cilia along the central canal.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Some motile cilia brush and interact with the fiber.
source: We observed in streaming acquisitions of RF and cilia labeled in GFP that some motile cilia brush and interact with the fiber.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion.

claim: Motile cilia from different fish have different beating frequencies in response to RF photoablation.
source: Accordingly, we measured that motile cilia from different fish have different beating frequencies in response to RF photoablation.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion.

claim: RF interacts with motile cilia, a mechanism that can lead to a reduction of ciliary beating as well as to friction between RF and the cilia.
source: Altogether, our observations indicate that RF interacts with motile cilia, a mechanism that can lead to a reduction of ciliary beating as well as to friction between RF and the cilia.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on observations.

claim: The impact of RF ablation on cilia beating frequency is still elusive.
source: The impact of RF ablation on cilia beating frequency is still elusive, which is consistent with our previous observations that the absence of a fiber did not lead to a massive change in particle velocity profile in the embryo (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The fiber could slightly alter the CSF flow profile in a transverse section by adding a point of null flow at the center of the central canal.
source: However, the fiber could nonetheless slightly alter the CSF flow profile in a transverse section by adding a point of null flow at the center of the central canal.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion.

claim: Adding a point of null velocity can increase the velocity gradient in the CSF, and thereby increase the phenomenon of shearing at the level of the CSF-cN apical extension.
source: Adding a point of null velocity can increase the velocity gradient in the CSF, and thereby increase the phenomenon of shearing at the level of the CSF-cN apical extension - in line with their functional coupling as reported was critical to mediate mechanoreception in vivo (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The Reissner fiber radius is ~100 nm.
source: Since the Reissner fiber radius is ~100 nm (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2020), our resolution to identify the center of the fiber with classical fluorescent microscopy is certainly limited.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Acute ablation of the Reissner fiber reduced the spontaneous calcium activity of CSF-cNs.
source: Nonetheless, we showed here that acute ablation of the Reissner fiber reduced the spontaneous calcium activity of CSF-cNs, indicating that a functional coupling may exist as well when the fiber spontaneously oscillates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on experimental results.

claim: A functional coupling may exist between RF and CSF-cNs when the fiber spontaneously oscillates.
source: Nonetheless, we showed here that acute ablation of the Reissner fiber reduced the spontaneous calcium activity of CSF-cNs, indicating that a functional coupling may exist as well when the fiber spontaneously oscillates.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion based on experimental results.

claim: The fiber's vertical movement along the dorsoventral axis could lead to contact with the CSF-cN apical extension to enhance the spontaneous calcium activity of the ventrally located sensory neurons.
source: The fiber's vertical movement along the dorsoventral axis could lead to contact with the CSF-cN apical extension to enhance the spontaneous calcium activity of the ventrally located sensory neurons we measured here.
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion.

claim: Interactions with dorsally located sensory neurons may occur as well due to displacement in the horizontal plane, but were more difficult to image and report on in the experimental conditions.
source: Interactions with dorsally located sensory neurons may occur as well due to displacement in the horizontal plane, but were more difficult to image and report on in our conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: The axial sensory system could form around the oscillating fiber and lead to the observed noise in the neuronal activity in resting baseline position.
source: The axial sensory system could form around the oscillating fiber and lead to the observed noise in the neuronal activity in resting baseline position (Sternberg et al., 2018; Prendergast et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included slowing down of locomotion (a reduction of locomotor frequency and amplitude).
source: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included slowing down of locomotion (a reduction of locomotor frequency and amplitude, Böhm et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021), postural defects during fast locomotion (rolling, Hubbard et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021) as well as morphological defects of the body axis in the embryo (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and the spine in juvenile/adult fish (Sternberg et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included postural defects during fast locomotion (rolling).
source: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included slowing down of locomotion (a reduction of locomotor frequency and amplitude, Böhm et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021), postural defects during fast locomotion (rolling, Hubbard et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021) as well as morphological defects of the body axis in the embryo (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and the spine in juvenile/adult fish (Sternberg et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included morphological defects of the body axis in the embryo.
source: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included slowing down of locomotion (a reduction of locomotor frequency and amplitude, Böhm et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021), postural defects during fast locomotion (rolling, Hubbard et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021) as well as morphological defects of the body axis in the embryo (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and the spine in juvenile/adult fish (Sternberg et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included morphological defects of the spine in juvenile/adult fish.
source: In zebrafish with genetic mutations, silencing or acute manipulations affecting CSF-cN activity or the maintenance of the Reissner fiber, sensorimotor deficits included slowing down of locomotion (a reduction of locomotor frequency and amplitude, Böhm et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021), postural defects during fast locomotion (rolling, Hubbard et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021) as well as morphological defects of the body axis in the embryo (Cantaut-Belarif et al., 2018) and the spine in juvenile/adult fish (Sternberg et al., 2018; Troutwine et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Multiple studies in mice indicate that CSF-cN-dependent functions for sensorimotor integration during locomotion observed in zebrafish are conserved in mammals.
source: Multiple studies in mice indicate that CSF-cN-dependent functions for sensorimotor integration during locomotion observed in zebrafish are conserved in mammals (Gerstmann et al., 2022; Nakamura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The SCOspondin gene SSPOP is a pseudogene in humans.
source: The SCOspondin gene SSPOP is a pseudogene in humans (https://www-ncbi-nlm-nih-gov/gene/23145), supporting the hypothesis that the Reissner fiber is absent in humans and great apes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The Reissner fiber is absent in humans and great apes.
source: The SCOspondin gene SSPOP is a pseudogene in humans (https://www-ncbi-nlm-nih-gov/gene/23145), supporting the hypothesis that the Reissner fiber is absent in humans and great apes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis supported by the pseudogene status of SSPOP.
